name: Original sin and predestination (the anti-Pelagian doctrine of salvation)
plain_explanation: Because Adam and Eve sinned, all their descendants inherit a corrupted nature and deserve eternal damnation; no one can, by their own effort, be virtuous enough to earn salvation. God, however, freely and unaccountably chooses some people (the elect) to receive the grace that saves them, while leaving the rest to the damnation everyone equally deserves.
precise_definition: The doctrine that Adam's sin corrupted all humanity, that all deserve eternal damnation (including unbaptized infants), that no one can abstain from sin without God's grace, and that God, by an unmotivated choice not based on merit, elects certain baptized persons to salvation while leaving the rest justly damned -- damnation displaying God's justice, salvation His mercy.
why_it_mattered: It was Augustine's answer to Pelagius's claim that virtuous moral effort alone could earn salvation, and it became, via Calvin, the doctrine of predestination central to Reformed Protestantism, while being explicitly rejected in this extreme form by the later Catholic Church.
historical_origin: Worked out across Augustine's controversial writings against Pelagius and his followers (the Pelagian controversy), and grounded, in Augustine's own reading, in the Pauline Epistle to the Romans.
examples: Augustine's claim, in the Confessions, to have been guilty of sins even in the cradle
The doctrine that unbaptized infants who die are damned to hell
objections: Russell notes the one difficulty that genuinely troubled Augustine himself: if original sin passes from Adam, the soul as well as the body must be propagated by the parents, though sin belongs to the soul, not the body -- a problem Augustine leaves undecided since Scripture is silent
competing_positions: Pelagius's doctrine of free will and salvation by moral effort
Semi-Pelagianism, a weakened compromise position condemned at the Council of Orange (529)
influence_on_later_thinkers: Revived by Calvin at the Reformation; its eschatology, if not its full theocratic doctrine, remained influential among Anabaptists, Fifth Monarchy Men, and Quakers.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly theological, with Russell noting its influence on the 'gloomy sense of universal guilt' he holds partly responsible for the ferocity of the medieval Church.
